before.supportingExcerpt: Source classes: cfDNA is DNA outside intact cells in a sample, and ctDNA is the tumour-derived part of that pool, so the two are related materials and not rival tests. In healthy donors a methylation atlas of 25 tissues and cell types attributed plasma cfDNA to white blood cells (55%), erythrocyte progenitors (30%), vascular endothelial cells (10%) and hepatocytes (1%) (Moss 2018). A tumour adds DNA only when it contributes, and the tumour share may be small or absent in the sample drawn even when cancer exists elsewhere.

before.supportingExcerpt: Scale: plasma DNA fragments show a pattern reminiscent of nuclease-cleaved nucleosomes with a peak at 166 base pairs (Lo 2010, in maternal plasma), and tumour-derived fragments are enriched at 90 to 150 base pairs (Mouliere 2018). One assay input in a breast-cancer comparison was 4,500 amplifiable copies, about 15 nanograms (Santonja 2023), and at about 3.3 picograms per haploid genome copy 1 nanogram is roughly 300 copies (arithmetic from genome size). In a fictional single-locus model with 4,500 amplifiable opportunities and target-allele probability 1 in 100,000, the expected target count is 0.045. The target-allele probability is not automatically a tumour-DNA fraction: copy number, variant multiplicity and clone representation matter.

before.supportingExcerpt: Detection depends on stage and tumour type: with digital PCR-based methods in 640 patients, ctDNA was found in more than 75% of people with advanced pancreatic, ovarian, colorectal, bladder, gastro-oesophageal, breast, melanoma, hepatocellular and head and neck cancers, and in fewer than 50% of primary brain, renal, prostate or thyroid cancers. The assay, specimen and population are part of each figure.

after.supportingExcerpt: ctDNA is a subset of cell-free DNA, and not every plasma variant is tumour-derived. Razavi's 2019 study enrolled 124 people with metastatic cancer and 47 controls without cancer. In the Results source analysis, 918 of 1,727 cfDNA mutations (53.2%) in non-hypermutated cancer samples and 297 of 364 (81.6%) in controls were also found in white blood cells and interpreted as likely clonal haematopoiesis. These are mutation-level fractions in those analysis groups, not percentages of all patients or all possible cancer samples. A ctDNA result is also a quantity with a unit, such as molecules per millilitre, a fraction or a call; the same printed number means different things under each.

Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess its origin; some variants remain ambiguous. before.supportingExcerpt: Collection conditions can change the mixture before testing: blood-cell breakdown adds genomic DNA and can dilute a tumour fraction. The NCI biospecimen practices document, revised February 2025, prefers plasma to serum. Its protocol recommends EDTA, accepts acid citrate dextrose, and advises avoiding heparin and citrate; the literature-summary section separately reports results with several anticoagulants when processing was immediate. For EDTA blood the protocol prefers centrifugation within 2 hours and accepts up to 4 hours at room temperature or 24 hours at 4 degrees Celsius; it recommends stabilising tubes for anticipated delays over 2 hours. These are recommendations for that specimen workflow, not a universal acceptance rule for every assay. Extraction and library preparation then retain only some available molecules, so the volume drawn is not the volume evaluated.

before.supportingExcerpt: Reading an assay report starts with the specimen and collection date, the plasma volume actually evaluated, DNA quality and recovery, origin checks, and the rule that turns a signal into a call. Low shedding, damaged input or failed quality controls can limit interpretation; a failed assay is a separate result from no qualifying signal. Genotyping, response monitoring and residual-disease detection are different intended uses. In its November 2024 drug-development guidance, FDA asks for validation of the complete workflow, representative clinical samples, the input range and prespecified calling cut-offs; validation of one use does not establish another.

before.supportingExcerpt: Collection conditions can change the mixture before testing: blood-cell breakdown adds genomic DNA and can dilute a tumour fraction. The NCI biospecimen practices document, revised February 2025, prefers plasma to serum. Its protocol recommends EDTA, accepts acid citrate dextrose, and advises avoiding heparin and citrate; the literature-summary section separately reports results with several anticoagulants when processing was immediate. For EDTA blood the protocol prefers centrifugation within 2 hours and accepts up to 4 hours at room temperature or 24 hours at 4 degrees Celsius; it recommends stabilising tubes for anticipated delays over 2 hours. These are recommendations for that specimen workflow, not a universal acceptance rule for every assay. Extraction and library preparation then retain only some available molecules, so the volume drawn is not the volume evaluated.

before.supportingExcerpt: Reading an assay report starts with the specimen and collection date, the plasma volume actually evaluated, DNA quality and recovery, origin checks, and the rule that turns a signal into a call. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess its origin; some variants remain ambiguous. after.supportingExcerpt: A TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from a tumour or from a therapy-selected blood-cell clone. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess origin, but some variants remain ambiguous. Razavi's 2019 study enrolled 124 people with metastatic cancer and 47 controls. In its Results source analysis, 918 of 1,727 cfDNA mutations (53.2%) in non-hypermutated cancer samples and 297 of 364 (81.6%) in controls were blood-cell matched and interpreted as likely clonal haematopoiesis. Those are mutation-level fractions in the stated analysis groups. The methods also kept an ambiguous category when sequencing depth could not establish different allele frequencies in plasma and blood cells, even without positive evidence of the variant in blood cells. Subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.

before.supportingExcerpt: Clonal haematopoiesis (CH) is the broader phenomenon of blood-cell clones carrying acquired changes. In the 2022 WHO myeloid classification, CHIP requires a somatic mutation in a myeloid-malignancy-associated gene at a variant allele fraction of at least 2%, or at least 4% for X-linked gene mutations in males, without a diagnosed haematological disorder or unexplained cytopenia (Khoury 2022). Persistent unexplained cytopenia changes the classification question. These are criteria for a named category, not a rule that every smaller blood-cell clone is absent, tumour-derived or a sequencing error.

before.supportingExcerpt: Reading the figures: a variant allele fraction counts variant alleles among the alleles evaluated and is not automatically the percentage of cells. Acquired (somatic) means not inherited and does not mean malignant. There is no age at which a plasma variant can simply be dismissed. Sequential samples show clones with DNA-damage-response mutations outgrowing others after radiation, platinum or topoisomerase II inhibitor exposure (Bolton 2020), which is selection of clones that can already be present and does not mean every new detection was caused by treatment.

before.supportingExcerpt: Fictional example: a plasma assay detects a variant that sensitive matched blood-cell sequencing finds at 0.8% VAF. The blood result supports a blood-cell contribution even below the 2% cut-off, but it does not make the variant CHIP or exclude a tumour contribution, because tumour evidence, shared variants and each method's limits still apply. Matched sequencing has its own gene coverage, depth and detection rules, so a clone below its sensitivity can stay unseen, and a clone finding is not a leukaemia diagnosis or a solid-tumour treatment instruction.

before.supportingExcerpt: Which genes: in blood-cell exomes from 17,182 people most clonal variants fell in DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1, were rare before age 40, and were seen in 9.5% of people aged 70 to 79 (Jaiswal 2014). ASXL1 mutations were enriched in current or former smokers, and radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitors selected for DNA-damage-response genes (TP53, PPM1D, CHEK2), with sequential samples showing those clones outgrowing others after exposure (Bolton 2020). In 8,810 people with non-haematological cancers, PPM1D and TP53 mutations were associated with prior chemotherapy, and clonal haematopoiesis was found in 25% (Coombs 2017).

before.supportingExcerpt: Clonal haematopoiesis (CH) is the broader phenomenon of blood-cell clones carrying acquired changes. In the 2022 WHO myeloid classification, CHIP requires a somatic mutation in a myeloid-malignancy-associated gene at a variant allele fraction of at least 2%, or at least 4% for X-linked gene mutations in males, without a diagnosed haematological disorder or unexplained cytopenia (Khoury 2022). Persistent unexplained cytopenia changes the classification question. These are criteria for a named category, not a rule that every smaller blood-cell clone is absent, tumour-derived or a sequencing error.

before.supportingExcerpt: Source attribution in plasma, interpretation rule: TP53 is a tumour gene and also a therapy-selected blood-cell gene, so a TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from either compartment. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess its origin; some variants remain ambiguous. In Razavi's paired sequencing 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 controls without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, and variants that could not be separated from white-blood-cell DNA kept an explicit ambiguous category, so subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.
before.explanation: Blood contribution, ambiguous source and the sensitivity/coverage of matched controls are explicit, without a perfect certificate. Source scope: Complete primary abstract confirms 124/47 and 53.2%/81.6%; earlier explicit ambiguous-category assessment is retained, not a perfect subtraction rule.

after.supportingExcerpt: A TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from a tumour or from a therapy-selected blood-cell clone. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess origin, but some variants remain ambiguous. Razavi's 2019 study enrolled 124 people with metastatic cancer and 47 controls. In its Results source analysis, 918 of 1,727 cfDNA mutations (53.2%) in non-hypermutated cancer samples and 297 of 364 (81.6%) in controls were blood-cell matched and interpreted as likely clonal haematopoiesis. Those are mutation-level fractions in the stated analysis groups. The methods also kept an ambiguous category when sequencing depth could not establish different allele frequencies in plasma and blood cells, even without positive evidence of the variant in blood cells. Subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.
after.explanation: Blood contribution, ambiguous source and the sensitivity/coverage of matched controls are explicit, without a perfect certificate. Source scope: Complete primary abstract confirms 124/47 and 53.2%/81.6%; earlier explicit ambiguous-category assessment is retained, not a perfect subtraction rule. P54 explicitly corrects the prior Razavi population-denominator shorthand and source-ambiguity wording against the Results/Methods passages; requirement and grade remain, without blanket source-depth promotion.

before.supportingExcerpt: Fictional example: a plasma assay detects a variant that sensitive matched blood-cell sequencing finds at 0.8% VAF. The blood result supports a blood-cell contribution even below the 2% cut-off, but it does not make the variant CHIP or exclude a tumour contribution, because tumour evidence, shared variants and each method's limits still apply. Matched sequencing has its own gene coverage, depth and detection rules, so a clone below its sensitivity can stay unseen, and a clone finding is not a leukaemia diagnosis or a solid-tumour treatment instruction.

before.supportingExcerpt: A gene name does not settle a plasma variant's source. Shah and colleagues found TP53 to be the most frequently mutated gene in their 2012 primary triple-negative breast-cancer cohort; Bolton's 2020 study found that radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitor exposure selected blood-cell clones with TP53 and other DNA-damage-response mutations. Those are different populations and compartments. A tumour reference and a matched blood-cell comparison help answer different questions, each within its own coverage and sensitivity. A newly confirmed tumour alteration can also reflect evolution rather than a blood-cell clone or technical noise.

before.supportingExcerpt: Scale: plasma DNA fragments show a pattern reminiscent of nuclease-cleaved nucleosomes with a peak at 166 base pairs (Lo 2010, in maternal plasma), and tumour-derived fragments are enriched at 90 to 150 base pairs (Mouliere 2018). One assay input in a breast-cancer comparison was 4,500 amplifiable copies, about 15 nanograms (Santonja 2023), and at about 3.3 picograms per haploid genome copy 1 nanogram is roughly 300 copies (arithmetic from genome size). In a fictional single-locus model with 4,500 amplifiable opportunities and target-allele probability 1 in 100,000, the expected target count is 0.045. The target-allele probability is not automatically a tumour-DNA fraction: copy number, variant multiplicity and clone representation matter.

before.supportingExcerpt: Collection conditions can change the mixture before testing: blood-cell breakdown adds genomic DNA and can dilute a tumour fraction. The NCI biospecimen practices document, revised February 2025, prefers plasma to serum. Its protocol recommends EDTA, accepts acid citrate dextrose, and advises avoiding heparin and citrate; the literature-summary section separately reports results with several anticoagulants when processing was immediate. For EDTA blood the protocol prefers centrifugation within 2 hours and accepts up to 4 hours at room temperature or 24 hours at 4 degrees Celsius; it recommends stabilising tubes for anticipated delays over 2 hours. These are recommendations for that specimen workflow, not a universal acceptance rule for every assay. Extraction and library preparation then retain only some available molecules, so the volume drawn is not the volume evaluated.

before.supportingExcerpt: Clonal haematopoiesis (CH) is the broader phenomenon of blood-cell clones carrying acquired changes. In the 2022 WHO myeloid classification, CHIP requires a somatic mutation in a myeloid-malignancy-associated gene at a variant allele fraction of at least 2%, or at least 4% for X-linked gene mutations in males, without a diagnosed haematological disorder or unexplained cytopenia (Khoury 2022). Persistent unexplained cytopenia changes the classification question. These are criteria for a named category, not a rule that every smaller blood-cell clone is absent, tumour-derived or a sequencing error.

before.supportingExcerpt: Which genes: in blood-cell exomes from 17,182 people most clonal variants fell in DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1, were rare before age 40, and were seen in 9.5% of people aged 70 to 79 (Jaiswal 2014). ASXL1 mutations were enriched in current or former smokers, and radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitors selected for DNA-damage-response genes (TP53, PPM1D, CHEK2), with sequential samples showing those clones outgrowing others after exposure (Bolton 2020). In 8,810 people with non-haematological cancers, PPM1D and TP53 mutations were associated with prior chemotherapy, and clonal haematopoiesis was found in 25% (Coombs 2017).

after.supportingExcerpt: A TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from a tumour or from a therapy-selected blood-cell clone. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess origin, but some variants remain ambiguous. Razavi's 2019 study enrolled 124 people with metastatic cancer and 47 controls. In its Results source analysis, 918 of 1,727 cfDNA mutations (53.2%) in non-hypermutated cancer samples and 297 of 364 (81.6%) in controls were blood-cell matched and interpreted as likely clonal haematopoiesis. Those are mutation-level fractions in the stated analysis groups. The methods also kept an ambiguous category when sequencing depth could not establish different allele frequencies in plasma and blood cells, even without positive evidence of the variant in blood cells. Subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.

These are criteria for a named category, not a rule that every smaller blood-cell clone is absent, tumour-derived or a sequencing error.

Matched sequencing has its own gene coverage, depth and detection rules, so a clone below its sensitivity can stay unseen, and a clone finding is not a leukaemia diagnosis or a solid-tumour treatment instruction.

before.supportingExcerpt: Scale: plasma DNA fragments show a pattern reminiscent of nuclease-cleaved nucleosomes with a peak at 166 base pairs (Lo 2010, in maternal plasma), and tumour-derived fragments are enriched at 90 to 150 base pairs (Mouliere 2018). One assay input in a breast-cancer comparison was 4,500 amplifiable copies, about 15 nanograms (Santonja 2023), and at about 3.3 picograms per haploid genome copy 1 nanogram is roughly 300 copies (arithmetic from genome size). In a fictional single-locus model with 4,500 amplifiable opportunities and target-allele probability 1 in 100,000, the expected target count is 0.045. The target-allele probability is not automatically a tumour-DNA fraction: copy number, variant multiplicity and clone representation matter.

before.supportingExcerpt: A gene name does not settle a plasma variant's source. Shah and colleagues found TP53 to be the most frequently mutated gene in their 2012 primary triple-negative breast-cancer cohort; Bolton's 2020 study found that radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitor exposure selected blood-cell clones with TP53 and other DNA-damage-response mutations. Those are different populations and compartments. A tumour reference and a matched blood-cell comparison help answer different questions, each within its own coverage and sensitivity. A newly confirmed tumour alteration can also reflect evolution rather than a blood-cell clone or technical noise.

after.supportingExcerpt: A gene name does not settle a plasma variant's source. Shah and colleagues found TP53 to be the most frequently mutated gene in their 2012 primary triple-negative breast-cancer cohort; Bolton's 2020 study found that radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitor exposure selected blood-cell clones with TP53 and other DNA-damage-response mutations. A newly confirmed tumour alteration can also reflect evolution rather than a blood-cell clone or technical noise.

before.supportingExcerpt: Source attribution in plasma, interpretation rule: TP53 is a tumour gene and also a therapy-selected blood-cell gene, so a TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from either compartment. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess its origin; some variants remain ambiguous. In Razavi's paired sequencing 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 controls without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, and variants that could not be separated from white-blood-cell DNA kept an explicit ambiguous category, so subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.

after.supportingExcerpt: A TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from a tumour or from a therapy-selected blood-cell clone. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess origin, but some variants remain ambiguous. Razavi's 2019 study enrolled 124 people with metastatic cancer and 47 controls. In its Results source analysis, 918 of 1,727 cfDNA mutations (53.2%) in non-hypermutated cancer samples and 297 of 364 (81.6%) in controls were blood-cell matched and interpreted as likely clonal haematopoiesis. Those are mutation-level fractions in the stated analysis groups. The methods also kept an ambiguous category when sequencing depth could not establish different allele frequencies in plasma and blood cells, even without positive evidence of the variant in blood cells. Subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.

before.supportingExcerpt: Source attribution in plasma, interpretation rule: TP53 is a tumour gene and also a therapy-selected blood-cell gene, so a TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from either compartment. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess its origin; some variants remain ambiguous. In Razavi's paired sequencing 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 controls without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, and variants that could not be separated from white-blood-cell DNA kept an explicit ambiguous category, so subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.

after.supportingExcerpt: A TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from a tumour or from a therapy-selected blood-cell clone. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess origin, but some variants remain ambiguous. Razavi's 2019 study enrolled 124 people with metastatic cancer and 47 controls. In its Results source analysis, 918 of 1,727 cfDNA mutations (53.2%) in non-hypermutated cancer samples and 297 of 364 (81.6%) in controls were blood-cell matched and interpreted as likely clonal haematopoiesis. Those are mutation-level fractions in the stated analysis groups. The methods also kept an ambiguous category when sequencing depth could not establish different allele frequencies in plasma and blood cells, even without positive evidence of the variant in blood cells. Subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.
